newsitem.title: USA: U.S. debt futures finish sharply higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. debt futures finish sharply higher.

text.p: U.S. debt futures closed sharply higher, convincing some traders and analysts that U.S. T-bonds are heading higher in the long term.

"The dynamics of the market could be seen in the same context as in November 1994," James Grauer, president of Omnitrage, said, referring to the T-bond market's 13-month rally that started in late 1994.

Friday's rally initially started from asset allocation out of stocks and into T-bonds, but later spiraled into a technical frenzy that pushed the lead September contract towards its three-month high of 110-09/32.
September T-bonds got as high as 109-26/32 on Friday, above the 200-day moving average of 109-23/32.
Technicals overshadowed fundamentals through the course of the day, feeding ideas that September T-bonds would rise to the 114-00 area by the end of summer, traders said.
Grauer said monthly stochastics had reached their lowest levels since 1994, and were now poised to cross higher. He said weekly stochastics crossed higher three weeks ago.
"When it crosses over in oversold markets that is a clear and irrefutable signal to an upside move," Grauer said.
"When it correlates with monthly upcrosses, now we're talking," he said. Monthly stochastics have only been at these low levels four times since 1977, he said.
Grauer said the November 1994 rally started after the U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates three-quarters of a point after a series of smaller rate hikes .

"If the Fed does bump up rates a half-a-point in July, it would replicate the same expectations as in November 1994," Grauer said, adding that inflation hawks would be satisfied with the Federal Reserve's vigilance.
"It's not been exactly responding negatively since the Fed raised rates in March," he said. The market also did not react positively after the Fed left rates unchanged on May 20.

He said preliminary estimates for U.S. first-quarter gross domestic product indicated that U.S. economic growth remained good. GDP was revised to show a gain of 5.8 percent, slightly above the 5.6 percent first reported, and compared with average trade estimates for 6.0 percent.
The final May University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey also rose slightly, while U.S. March new home sales were upwardly revised. April sales fell more than expected.

Speculation that U.S. payrolls numbers will be downwardly revised, coupled with comments from New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough, provided the catalyst for the stong upmove, traders said.
McDonough said around midsession that second-quarter economic information pointed to a slowdown in the U.S. economy.

At the end of pit trade, September T-bonds were up 23/32 at 109-20/32, and 10-year notes were up 17/32 at 107-01/32. December Eurodollars were up 0.07 at 93.77, after rising to 93.83, near the March 7 high of 93.84.
